turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Monday, October 26. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Brazil has a president-elect, and he is not the one the bond market wanted.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term in yesterday's runoff, with roughly 51.8% of the vote at 100% counted, a margin of about 4.4 million votes over Flávio Bolsonaro. Flávio led the first round, about 47% to 45%, and no candidate who trailed in round one had won a Brazilian runoff since 1989, so this is a genuine comeback.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And it is not a clean handoff. Flávio has not conceded, his camp is talking about annulment, and the sticking point is a last-minute extension of voting hours that a Supreme Court justice approved. Lula is inaugurated on January 5, so there are 10 weeks of noise ahead, and we will come to what the markets made of it in a few minutes.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Second story, and a bigger political earthquake than the polls suggested. In Serbia's snap parliamentary election, President Aleksandar Vučić went on television and conceded. His words: it is clear that we have lost these elections, the Student List has won.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The numbers are preliminary and they are his own. He projected the Student List at 135 to 140 of the 250 seats, his SNS around 105, and roughly 2.2 million votes for the students against 1.7 million for his party. He blamed independent media, European countries and what he called an American deep state, which is a familiar menu. He resigned the presidency on September 27 to run for prime minister, so a man who built a decade of Serbian politics around himself just lost the election he engineered.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Turnout was described as the highest in decades, and that is the part to remember. This was a protest movement, born in the student blockades after the 2024 Novi Sad canopy collapse, converted into votes. Whether Vučić's apparatus lets that conversion complete is the question for the coalition talks.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Iran now. President Trump said, in his words, the answer is no, there will not be a strike today, which leaves the option plainly open without exercising it. Outlets disagree on whether he said it Sunday or Monday, so treat the day loosely.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The diplomatic picture is more crowded than the rhetoric. Direct US-Iran talks are suspended, but Iran says contacts continue through intermediaries, Qatari mediators are in Tehran, and the names being floated for security talks there are Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan's Field Marshal Munir and Turkey's intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın. Hormuz remains the sticking point, and that is why Brent is where it is.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One more political date to circle. Israelis vote tomorrow, Tuesday, and the final polling averages have the opposition bloc around 51 seats and Netanyahu's bloc around 51, with neither near the 61 of 120 needed. Benny Gantz's former ally Gadi Eisenkot has his Yashar party ahead of Likud in most polls, roughly 20 to 23 seats against 18 to 21, and a party like Winter's People of Israel hovering at the 3.25% threshold could decide who forms a government.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which means exit polls tomorrow at 10 p.m. local time and a coalition negotiation that will last weeks, not hours.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: American Express said Friday it is cutting about 5% of its global workforce, roughly 3,500 jobs, with a $336 million restructuring charge. The CFO, Christophe Le Caillec, said the aim is a leaner, more agile company, and he explicitly said to prepare for AI.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The quarter itself was good, which is what makes the layoff notable. Adjusted EPS was $4.68 against about $4.48 expected, with GAAP EPS of $5.42 flattered by a $982 million pre-tax gain on the sale of its stake in the travel business GBT. Revenue slightly missed, and the stock fell about 3.6%, so the market read the cuts as a sign that the top line is not doing the work.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: It is the second AI-flavoured white-collar layoff headline in a week after Netflix, and the pattern is a profitable company cutting 5% while guiding up on earnings. That is the template for the next year of restructuring.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The counter-move on Friday was cybersecurity. After US agencies warned about vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, CrowdStrike jumped 8.25% and Palo Alto Networks 7.22%, with four cyber names taking the top-gainer slots on a day the Dow lost more than 600 points.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Security stocks as the one place money hid on a bad Friday, because a vulnerability warning is, perversely, a sales call.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: One deal from earlier in the week that is worth a line. Salesforce agreed on October 20 to buy the marketing-software firm Braze for 47.50 dollars a share in cash, an enterprise value of about 5.66 billion dollars and a premium near 58%. Braze jumped about 51% while Salesforce slipped 1.4%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The detail that stings is that 47.50 is still below the 65-dollar price at which Braze went public, so the premium is real and the round trip for IPO buyers is still underwater. Closing is expected in Salesforce's fiscal 2028, which gives antitrust and the market a long runway.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Brazilian market reaction started before Brazil's market opened. CME's real-dollar futures were up roughly 10% on Sunday evening, a Tokyo-listed Ibovespa ETF dropped somewhere between 11% and 15% depending on the outlet, and the US-listed EWZ was down 16% to 18% intraday.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: For scale, the Ibovespa closed Friday near 205,083 and the real was around 4.98 to the dollar. Analysts were warning of a drop of 7% or more in the real and a 10% fall in the index at the open, which would trip circuit breakers. I could not confirm a Monday close as we recorded, so treat all of this as the overnight signal, not the settled level.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The fear is fiscal. A Citi survey found most investors expected the real to lose at least 5% on a Lula win, and the argument is that a fourth term with a fractious Congress and a contested opposition leaves the spending-rule credibility question open. The counterpoint is that a lot of that was priced into the pre-election run-up, and one Rio morning call described the early open as cautious, not panicked.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story, private equity in life sciences. EQT has offered 46.50 euros a share for Qiagen, about 9.6 billion euros in equity, around 12.1 billion dollars including roughly 1.1 billion of net debt, with ADIA and CPP Investments affiliates co-investing.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The premium is only 8.6% to the last close, which is thin, and some holders are already calling it too low. Qiagen suspended its 2026 guidance, which reads as a company preparing to be private, and the deal is not expected to close until mid-2027. Thermo Fisher's roughly 11.5 billion dollar bid for Qiagen in 2020 failed on shareholder support, and that history is exactly why the premium will be tested.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Friday tape was not the story, and every level is on the Markets tab. The story is that oil displaced AI as the thing the market is afraid of. Brent settled at 116.72 dollars, up 3.14% on the day and about 6% on the week, its third straight weekly gain and the highest settle since late April.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the cause is physical, not rhetorical. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites, the Aramco headquarters evacuation in Dhahran, attacks on ships leaving Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate rose about 3.8% to 103.27. When crude is up 6% in a week, the 10-year Treasury sitting at 5.00% stops being an AI-worry yield and becomes an inflation-and-term-premium yield.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Dow lost more than 650 points, down 1.23%, which is a near miss on our threshold, and Nasdaq had its biggest one-day drop since June on Thursday before chips steadied on Friday. Elsewhere the quiet closes hide a weekly story: Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell about 4.5% on the week and gold dropped about 3.8%, breaking below 4,000 dollars at one point.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The week ahead is the real event. Microsoft and Alphabet report Wednesday after the close, Amazon Thursday, and the Fed decides Wednesday afternoon. The odds of a hike this meeting are under 10%, but roughly 80% is priced for December, which means the press conference is about the path, not the decision.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The setup is awkward for the equity bulls. Q3 earnings growth is on pace for more than 32% year over year, yet the multiple is being fought by a 5% 10-year and 117-dollar oil. If the hyperscalers guide capex up again, the market has to decide whether it is buying growth or financing it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Also worth watching is the Bank of Japan on October 30, and SK Hynix and Intel on the 29th, because memory is where the AI trade has been breaking.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Our deep dive today comes from this week's Economist. The Thursday leader is headlined "Saudi Arabia and the UAE are sowing chaos," with the subtitle that the Gulf powers should stop fuelling carnage in their backyard. We only have the newsletter blurb and open reporting, not the full paywalled text, so we are presenting the thesis as the Economist frames it and filling the substance from public sources.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The thesis is that the two states that used to run the Gulf as a bloc are now fighting a proxy contest across the Red Sea, even though each faces what the Economist calls massive crises close to home. They are spending power abroad, and that spending is stoking some of the worst wars on earth, Sudan and Yemen. For this audience the point is that the Red Sea corridor, shipping insurance and Saudi Arabia's own security are exposed to a rift between its two anchor partners.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Start with Sudan, because it is the clearest case. The United Arab Emirates is widely described as the main external backer of the Rapid Support Forces, while Saudi Arabia backs the Sudanese army. The army holds Khartoum and Port Sudan, the RSF holds Darfur after taking El Fasher in October 2025, and it is besieging El Obeid. A Saudi-brokered arms sale to the army was reportedly cancelled, which tells you how awkward the alignment is for Riyadh.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Yemen is where the rift went from quiet to kinetic. In December 2025 the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council launched an offensive in Hadramawt, and Riyadh responded by striking Mukalla and demanding that Abu Dhabi withdraw. The UAE announced a pullout, and the Council's gains were reversed. Sources conflict on whether the Council was dissolved or relaunched under a new name, and British parliamentary researchers note it still holds protests. Since mid-2026 the Houthi-Saudi front has also reopened.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So what is contested? First, whether this is a rupture or a managed rivalry. The Arab Reform Initiative's phrase for the Yemen episode was paused, not resolved, and few analysts expect the UAE to scale back its support for the RSF. Second, how much is Emirati choice and how much is Saudi overreach, because Riyadh has made its own strikes and its own demands.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Third, and this is where I would push back on the leader's framing, how much agency belongs to the Gulf at all. Sudan's generals, the RSF's commanders, Yemen's factions and their own economies of war all have interests that do not end when a patron changes its mind. A leader that says stop fuelling carnage assumes the tap can be turned off from Abu Dhabi, and the evidence from both wars is that it cannot.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The second-order read for this audience is energy and capital. Last week's Houthi strikes on Aramco facilities and the evacuation of the Dhahran headquarters were events. This is the structural explanation for why the Saudi security umbrella looks thinner than it did 2 years ago. If Saudi Arabia is fighting a Yemen front and managing an Emirati rival at once, its capacity to hold the Red Sea and the kingdom's giga-project funding gets squeezed in the same budget.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And for capital allocators the Gulf's role as the swing financier of AI infrastructure matters. Abu Dhabi's MGX and Riyadh's Humain are both underwriting data-centre builds, and a rivalry between the two sovereigns can show up as duplicated campuses, competing chip-allocation deals and political risk premia on deals that looked like a single Gulf bid.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The takeaway is that the Gulf is no longer a bloc you can price as one. The Economist's moral argument is that the carnage in Sudan and Yemen is a choice. The market argument is that the choice has a cost, and Brent at 116 dollars is a reminder of who pays.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Start with PJM, because the next 4 days matter. PJM has said it will file a revised Reliability Backstop Procurement at FERC by this Thursday, October 29, rather than wait out a hearing that would have run about 5 months. The reason is cost allocation: FERC found the framework flawed, and the Department of Energy on October 7 pushed for no cost shift onto existing customers.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: For reference, the original design was a one-time backstop auction to fill a 6.8 gigawatt shortfall, with terms up to 15 years and a maximum willingness to pay averaging 555 dollars per megawatt-day, with results targeted for December 2 ahead of the 2029-30 capacity auction. The refile leaves each PJM state to refine which retail loads bear the cost, so the fight moves to the statehouses.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There is a second filing, covering data-centre curtailment for large loads that come online after June 1, 2027. That is the sharper signal. It says the interconnection price for new campuses in PJM is a curtailment obligation, which changes how you underwrite a campus on a firm-service assumption. I would flag that these details come from trade reports before the filing, so check the actual docket on Thursday.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Utilities now. PG&E's Q3 shows a data-centre pipeline of 12,870 megawatts at the end of September against 12,710 in June, essentially flat, and it still targets 1.8 gigawatts online by 2030. The secondary summaries also say it trimmed its 2027 capex plan by about 2 billion dollars, and that is the line to verify, because it cuts against the story that every utility is raising capex.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: If it holds, the read is that the pipeline is not converting to ratebase growth, and the swing factor is California's wildfire-liability framework under SB 254. Capital goes where the regulatory return is credible, and a pipeline that does not clear the liability test does not get funded.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the compute side, two SemiAnalysis issues this week are worth a pointer, though we only saw previews. The October 23 piece argues Amazon's Trainium has moved from an inference chip to a credible training platform, with native PyTorch support and a more mature software stack, and the October 21 piece covers Huawei's Ascend 950PR and its tie to DeepSeek. The shared message is that accelerator supply is diversifying, which changes the power-density and cooling assumptions behind campus designs.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A quieter deal signal from the Dealflow newsletter: NiSource is tolling a 2,400 megawatt-hour battery while also building its own. Only the headline is visible, so no price or counterparty, but a utility renting storage while building storage suggests it needs capacity faster than its own construction schedule.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And context for the earnings that land this week. In its July 22 filing GE Vernova showed firm gas-turbine backlog rising from 44 to 53 gigawatts and slot reservations from 56 to 63, total 116 gigawatts, with a guide of at least 125 by year-end. We have taught the difference between reservations and firm orders, so the question for Wednesday and Thursday is how much of the hyperscaler capex, roughly 750 billion dollars across the group this year, is converting from reservation to firm.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Microsoft is guiding around 175 billion, Alphabet 195 to 205, Amazon about 220. If those numbers rise again with oil at 117 and the 10-year at 5%, the market will ask who funds the megawatts. That is the question that links this segment back to the tape.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Magandang umaga ulit. Ngayong umaga, dalawang salita ang pag-aaralan natin, at pareho silang galing sa balita tungkol sa badyet at sa piso.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang una ay isiningit. Ito ang anyong pasibo ng pandiwang isingit, at ang ibig sabihin nito ay inilagay nang palihim sa pagitan ng iba pang bagay. Kapag sinabi mong isiningit ang isang proyekto sa badyet, may pahiwatig na hindi ito dumaan sa tamang proseso.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Magkaiba ito sa inilagay o ipinasok. Ang inilagay ay neutral, parang simpleng paglalagay lang. Ang isiningit ay may kulay ng pagdududa, kaya madalas itong marinig sa mga balita tungkol sa pork barrel at mga kuwestiyonableng pondo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Halimbawa, isiningit daw sa badyet ng Department of Agriculture ang libu-libong proyekto. Napapansin mo ang salitang daw, na nagsasabing hindi pa ito napatutunayan. Ganyan ang tamang tono sa balita.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang ikalawang salita ay bumulusok. Ito ay pagbagsak na mabilis, matarik at tuloy-tuloy, parang ibong sumisid mula sa himpapawid. Mas matindi ito kaysa bumagsak, na simpleng pagbaba o pagkahulog lang.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Kaya sa pamagat ng balita, bumulusok ang halaga ng piso ay mas dramatiko kaysa bumaba ang piso. Ginagamit din ito sa panitikan, sa mga sumisid na agila o sa mga pangarap na bumulusok. Hindi mo ito sasabihin sa maliit na pagbabago, kundi sa pagbagsak na ramdam ng lahat.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Tandaan natin ang dalawa: isiningit para sa palihim na paglalagay, bumulusok para sa matarik na pagbagsak. Maririnig natin silang pareho sa susunod na segment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Isiningit daw ang halos 190 bilyong piso na halaga ng 7,054 na proyekto sa panukalang badyet ng Department of Agriculture para sa 2027, ayon sa People's Budget Coalition na humarap sa komite ng Senado noong Oktubre 21.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Bumulusok naman ang piso sa 63.95 kontra dolyar nitong Lunes, ang ikalimang sunod na rekord na pagsadsad, kahit tinaasan ng Bangko Sentral ang interes ng 50 basis points noong nakaraang linggo.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Samantala, may gantimpalang 50 milyong piso na ang ulo ni Senador Ronald dela Rosa, ayon sa DILG, at binigyan ng Philippine National Police ng isang linggong palugit ang senador na sumuko bago ang ika-30 ng Oktubre.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Let us go through the budget story in detail. The coalition says the DA's proposed 2027 budget is about 198.45 billion pesos, 8% below this year's 215.69 billion, yet the House inserted those 7,054 projects. Among them, 355 farm-to-market roads worth about 6 billion pesos were not in the President's proposed budget at all, and one 23 million peso road has coordinates that plot in the sea off Benham Rise, with others near Brunei and in the Celebes Sea.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Agriculture secretary, Francisco Tiu Laurel, blames misplaced decimals from manually transferred coordinates, and the coalition itself says the discrepancies are not proof of corruption. It does, however, call this flood-control scandal 2.0, and the senators now have the bicameral conference, which Senate President Sotto says will be livestreamed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The dela Rosa case is the other leg. He is wanted on an International Criminal Court warrant for murder as a crime against humanity, tied to at least 32 killings in the drug war, issued in November 2025 and made public in May. Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla called him armed and dangerous, the bounty is funded from DILG and police intelligence money, a task force is led by Major General Wilson Lopez, and the ultimatum lapses around October 30. His lawyers oppose the bounty, and the Senate minority bloc wants dialogue.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the economy, the peso is the transmission line. Governor Eli Remolona said on Friday that the BSP did not hike rates to defend the peso, it intervenes only against inflationary swings, and he will not disclose that threshold because it would help speculators. Counts of the record lows differ from outlet to outlet, so we will just say record after record.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the fiscal side is not helping. The national government deficit for January to September was 1.303 trillion pesos, up 16.6% from a year earlier, overshooting the 9-month programme by about 97 billion and using 78.56% of the 1.66 trillion full-year ceiling. September alone was 248.9 billion pesos. A weaker peso also raises the peso cost of foreign debt service, which is our inference, not a reported number.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The household version is Meralco. October's residential rate rose to 15.06 pesos per kilowatt-hour, up 32 centavos, with the generation charge up nearly 50 centavos on fuel, the peso and tight supply, so a typical 200-kilowatt-hour bill rises about 64 pesos.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, both from the China story we are about to tell, and both finance-desk language. The first is a connective, 倘若, and the second is a verb that shows up everywhere in economic writing, 依赖.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 倘若 means if or supposing that, and it is a written, formal conditional. It is more hypothetical and bookish than the neutral 如果, and it often pairs with 就 or 则 in the result clause. Here is the example: 倘若土地出让收入继续下滑，地方政府就很难偿还债务。(If land-sale income keeps sliding, local governments will struggle to repay their debts.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The contrast worth learning is with 一旦. 一旦 says once it happens, as if the event is coming, while 倘若 stays in the realm of suppose. In a finance column, 倘若 is the safer, more cautious hedge, the one an editor uses when the writer does not want to predict the outcome.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The second word, 依赖, means to depend on or rely on. It is formal-neutral, and in economics writing you see it as 依赖于 for the more abstract pattern. The example: 许多地方政府长期依赖土地财政。(Many local governments have long relied on land finance.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the near-synonym to separate it from is 取决于, which you will remember from earlier episodes. 取决于 describes what an outcome is determined by, a neutral cause. 依赖 describes dependence, and it usually carries a worried tone. So 经济增长取决于出口 is a statement of fact, while 经济增长依赖出口 sounds like a warning. (Growth is determined by exports, versus growth relies on exports.)

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A final note on collocation: 依赖 pairs with 进口, 出口, 补贴 and 土地财政, and it takes an object directly, so you do not need a preposition. Keep both words in your ear, because the next segment uses them.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 倘若土地出让收入继续下滑，地方政府就更难偿还债务，而许多地方政府长期依赖土地财政。(If land-sale income keeps sliding, local governments will find it harder still to repay their debts, and many have long relied on land finance.)

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That is the number behind the sentence. Land-sale revenue fell 27.9% year over year in January to September, according to the finance ministry data reported by Reuters and Caixin, and September alone was down 23.2%. The sharper question is how much of that remaining revenue is real, since local-government financing vehicles buying land inflate the figure, and one Renmin University estimate puts the true decline at 50% to 65%, which is a single outlier source.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The two-speed picture is clean here. General budget revenue rose 5.1% to 17.2 trillion yuan on exports and high-tech, while the land income that services local debt shrinks. Net special-bond issuance reached 3.56 trillion yuan, 81% of the annual quota, and officials plan to front-load part of next year's quota.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But spending is not following the borrowing. Nine-month spending execution was about 70% of the annual budget, the lowest in 6 years, so local governments are borrowing more and spending less, which is what a balance-sheet repair looks like when it is forced rather than chosen. Goldman estimates that the new home-sale rules would cut land-sale revenue by 30%, up from a previous 20% estimate.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The side note on markets is the yuan. It hit 6.6682 per dollar today, its strongest since June 2022, while the central bank set the fix 471 pips weaker than the market expected, which Barclays reads as the PBOC resisting rapid appreciation. A strong external side and a weak domestic side is the two-speed economy in one chart.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In Paris, a new private art centre called Large opened on October 17 on the Île Seguin, the former Renault factory island west of the city. The 5,000 square metre building is by RCR Arquitectes, the Catalan studio behind many Pritzker-winning projects, and the inaugural show is Imaginary Engine, directed by Cecilia Alemani, who ran the 2022 Venice Biennale.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The show has more than 100 works by 55 artists, about 50 from Renault's own collection and 17 new commissions, in 5 chapters that include The Factory of My Thoughts, Social Bodies and The Human Machine. It revisits Renault's late-1960s programme that paired artists with engineers, and it runs to March 7, 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The critic's question is whether a corporate-collection show on a brownfield factory site is a critique of industrial labour or a brand halo. I could not find a full critical review yet, so that is a question, not a verdict. But Alemani's track record is for curating tension, not tidy corporate celebration.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: In London, the Barbican has Robert Ryman: The Real Thing, running to February 28, the first in-depth UK look at the painter in more than 30 years. There are over 60 works, including a recreation of his studio wall in the Surface Veil works and the 12-panel Standard from 1967, never before shown in London.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The way to see Ryman is not as white on white as emptiness, but as an argument about the paint's own materials: the support, the fixings, the edge. Again, that is the exhibition's own framing and a standard reading, not a review.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two quick pointers for the weekend. ArtReview's verdict on British Art Show 10, published October 20, was the headline Polite Fury, and Frieze reviewed the Toronto Biennial on October 21. We have only seen the headlines, but the phrase polite fury is a fair description of a lot of institutional art right now.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First, Megan McArdle in the Washington Post on Sunday, headlined "Tax the billionaires. Watch them leave California." Proposition 40 is on the November 3 ballot, a one-time 5% tax on billionaires' accumulated wealth. As the headline signals, her argument is that the tax could raise billions or it could drive away the revenue base.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The steelman is that a one-time levy only works if assets cannot move, and a wealthy resident can relocate before the measure takes effect, so the headline figure is a ceiling and not a forecast. A tax that raises less than promised and costs future income tax revenue is worse than none.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The counter-take, and this is ours, not hers: the exit threat is weaker for people whose wealth sits in illiquid, California-anchored companies, and a measure voters want is not invalidated by a modelled leakage rate. We have only read the headline and standfirst, and one source lists her among the measure's endorsers, so treat her position as unconfirmed.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second, Jamie Fly and Jennifer Brody, also in the Post, on "The autocrats waging war on Starlink." The argument is that Tehran and Moscow are working to disrupt satellite internet and that Washington should respond.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The steelman is that satellite links are now the one channel that bypasses state shutdowns, so jamming them is censorship by other means and deserves a deterrent response. The counter-take is that the response depends on a single private company and its owner's discretion, so the policy risk is dependence on one vendor, which is a theme we heard in the Chinese vocab today.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last Monday in St. Paul, Minnesota, 27-year-old Ebro Ahmed was standing outside a store when a school bus rolled past with its doors open. The driver was apparently having a seizure, and about 18 middle schoolers from a Battle Creek Middle School route were aboard.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ahmed ran over, got the bus into neutral and set the parking brake, then called police and ambulances. Nobody was hurt, and the store's surveillance video backs up his account. He has no medical training, said Grey's Anatomy kept him calm, and told reporters, I really felt like it was my duty.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That is The Morning Commute for Monday, October 26. Thanks for listening, and we will see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Have a good week, and take the long way around the bad news.
